analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Number 95, Hoover Motor Express Company, versus United States of America, and number 109, Tank Truck Rettles, versus Commissioner of Internal Revenue. Mr. Sarner. Mr. Sarner, please, you'll recall that Mr. Hardwood was presenting the argument, part of the argument, on behalf of both these carriers, and he has a little time left. He'd like to reserve that until the end of the argument to resume his point. You will note that these cases involve the deductibility for income tax purposes of fines paid to various states for operating on the highways of these states, motor vehicles which exceeded the maximum weight or axle weight limitations prescribed by the states. They raise the problem with the Allied cases of Sullivan, Messi, and Ross of the use of a public policy rationale, or as the government is raising in the Allied cases, payments which are made to obtain the commission of a crime by the recipient as being excluded from this concept of ordinary and necessary business expenses for purposes of deduction. Of course, I think we'll all agree that the use of public policy, that to allow us, for example, to deduct these fines in some way remits, reduces the punishment, using it in the broad sense which the state has imposed upon us for exceeding these weight laws, or it's subsidiary that you can't deduct illegal payments. And I call your attention, Your Honors, that this is a subsidiary argument, a subsidiary rationale. Now, the reason why illegal payments, if they cannot be deducted, would depend again on the fact that it frustrates the policy of the state, which makes this activity for which the payment is made a particular crime or proscribes its commission. Of course, this has a smooth-sounding plausibility. I mean, it may shock all of us, most of us, that businessmen will transgress the law, and that when they're fined for this transgression, when they're so-called punished for the transgression, or when they want to make payments which are proscribed, which are designated possibly a crime, or some sort of prohibited activity, that the tax law should so recognize these payments as to allow the deductibility in computing the revenue, the amount which has to be paid to the government. But, Your Honors, this use of public policy, or this use of an illegal payment by the government in these cases, which has been, to some extent, as we'll see, developed in a very confusing way by the courts, is a completely foreign concept to the purposes, to the intendment of the Internal Revenue Code. I'd like, Your Honors, to look at page 21 of our brief. We quote what the Congress, what the Committee of Congress was considering when the original 1913 bill was passed after the enactment of the 16th Amendment. And at this time, it was suggested by Senator Sterling that there should be some amendments to the bill which would limit the deductibility of expenses and computing income to legal expenses, to a legal trade or business. And Senator Williams, who was a ranking member of the Committee at that time, said the object of this bill is... On page 21. Oh, 21, sorry. He said the object of this bill is to tax a man's net income. That is to say, what he has at the end of the year, after deducting from his receipts, his expenditures or losses, it is not to reform men's moral characters. That is not the object of the bill at all. The tax is not levied for the purpose of restraining people from betting on horse races or upon futures. But the tax is framed for the purpose of making a man pay upon his net income his actual profit during the year. The law does not care where he got it from so far as the tax is concerned, although the law may very properly care in another way. Now, I'm sure that my friends representing the respondents in Sullivan, Ross, and Messi will amplify this concept of the legislative history and the various times that there was sought by the Congress, by some members of Congress, to proscribe the concept of ordinary and necessary by a limitation that it can't be some sort of an illegal expense. And all of these times, this was rejected by the Congress. How do we know why Congress rejects a proposal? Well, we may not... How can you build... I don't know why I take it out of you. I hear these arguments frequently, sometimes from the government and sometimes the government opposes. But how do we know why an amendment is rejected? Well, we know in one sense, and so far in 1951, your honors will see when I'm sure the other counsel raised the point, Senator Keefoffer attempted to have an actual limitation on deductibility of expenses, denying any expenses incurred in the operation of illegal wagering or gambling. And the debates at that time point out that this actually would amount to a tax on gross income, not on net income, which is the impediment of the Revenue Act. It's not to enforce the particular penalty provisions or the public policies of the criminal laws of the states. They can take care of themselves. There are many effective ways to do that. And that the object of the income tax law, regardless of what may be the objects of other so-called revenue measures, is to produce the fair share of income which a man should pay. That's still... May I put this to you? Surely. When you say public policy, isn't it just as fair to put this problem as... We have to... Necessary isn't a self-defining concept. No, sir. Since I've been here any number of times, we had all sorts of questions of what is included in the concept of necessary. Isn't that the real question? So, whenever we come to define the limit or determine the content, what is within the content of necessary. What is it? Ordinary and necessary. Ordinary and necessary. Strange concept, conjunction of words, anyhow. Ordinary and necessary. Not that things may be ordinary, but are unnecessary, and vice versa. Whenever we come to define and determine what the content is, we have to take into consideration relevant factors. Positively. Now, if you call that public policy, all right. Well, I... There's no more different public policy than other questions. No, sir. I'm not saying it... That gives me the answer. It doesn't give me the answer. No. Well, I think I can give you the answer, Your Honor, and, of course, that's what I hope to do. I just don't want you to label it... No. ...as a contention of some extraneous consideration. Well, it is an extraneous consideration in the context that it's used by the respondent in this case, and, by the way, it's been used by the lower courts in our two cases. It's a completely foreign and extraneous concept, having no bounds, as we'll see, in any workable rule whatsoever. But I just... Before I... And I'll answer that in one moment. I do want to make one further point, because this runs through the... It seems to me through the entire government's position. They take the view that just because an expenditure is economically involved or integral, so intertwined with the production of the income, that in and of itself does not make the expense deductible as an ordinary and necessary business expense. We agree. The three-quarters of some of the arguments that are made are made on what I say is this straw premise. We don't deny that merely because an expenditure is economically involved in the production of income that it is automatically deductible. We admit that it must be ordinary and necessary. And here, in answer to Justice Frankfurter, I think we come to the point of the role that public policy, in the context that it's used by these courts and by the respondents, that in some way the state set forth a policy and to allow an income tax deduction of expenditures made, which may be in violation of that policy, frustrates, prevents, interferes with the state's enforcement. That's the sense that's used in this so-called public policy rationale. Mr. Sarner, may I ask you, however uncertain may be the meaning in this context of the words ordinary and necessary, does that same uncertainty obtain to the words business expense? Possibly the same, sure, I would say the same uncertainty does obtain, but I don't think, Your Honor, that there is this much uncertainty as to the meaning of ordinary and necessary business expenses. We have had, Your Honors, have decided a number of cases insofar as the business aspect is what is a business expense. The Kornhauser case points out that if it's approximately results from, is connected with, directly connected with the business, it is a business expense. Is there any case which holds that an expenditure made in violation of the law could be a business expense whether necessary and ordinary to the business or not? Well, it depends what you mean, Your Honor, in violation of law. In violation of law has a lot of different meanings. There have been cases, for example, well, you take the Ross-Sullivan and the messy cases which will be presented to you. Their expenditures under the government's view were made by the taxpayer engaged in illegal bookmaking, wagering, to employees in the expenditure itself, aside from the activity of the taxpayer being to get the employee to himself commit the crime. That's independently made a crime. Well, Seventh Circuit said that this is no question that this is a deductible ordinary, they admitted it was a business expense, it was a question of whether it was an ordinary or necessary expense. The same thing with respect to the rent in the Sullivan and Messy cases. But wasn't that a matter expressly covered by the code itself? Well, that's the taxpayer's argument that insofar as... Well, far as salaries and rent are concerned, the taxpayer says that, and I wouldn't want to take any position contrary to his, but I think that the government probably will point out to your honors that salaries and rents don't embrace anything further. These are just illustrative of typical types of business expenses, which have further limitations on them, that salaries must be reasonable, rent must be not connected with buying the business, buying the property, but merely for using it. I don't personally think that that is the touchstone, the fact that the code happens to designate salary or rent as such. But to come back to what Justice Franksford pointed out, in a big sense, public policy and illegality plays a very important part in what is ordinary and necessary. That is, when the law of a state where people are doing business proscribe certain conduct, when societies, for example, professional societies, frown upon certain conduct, this puts a general limitation on what people ordinarily and normally do. There is no doubt that if it's illegal to make certain types of payments, generally, in the business community, in the reputable business community, people will not make those certain types of payments. But the concept of, and to that extent, it plays into the concept of ordinary and necessary. Because ordinary, as your honors have pointed out in a number of cases, means common, frequent, normal, usual in this particular type of business. And I agree that in the normal, let us say, in the normal, legitimate business, it is unusual, it is not common, it is not frequent, to find that the taxpayer is bribing public officials to get state contracts, to find that the taxpayer is otherwise violating the law and his expenditures. And hence, it's not that the state proscribes this and says this is a criminal act or this is a penalty, we punish you for doing this. This sets the normal pattern of what people do in the business community, the community with which we are particularly interested. But this court has also pointed out, your honors, in the Lilly case, the Heininger case, you pointed out that what is ordinary and normal means for a particular business. And therefore, if you have in the gambler's cases, I have no doubt, if you have an illegal business, and you do have expenses which are integral and normal and common, assuming you work on the assumption that you do have the illegal business operating, the government for purposes of revenue, for tax purposes, is interested and so intended when it enacted the Revenue Act to take just the net amount of the income. Well, the government got the presupposition of this whole business with regard to gambling gains is that that's also a form of business, isn't it? Surely. Oh, yeah. And if it's a business, the government can't have it both ways. No, it can't. It's a business for one purpose and not for another. Well, that's exactly right. And Mr. Harwood, you may recall yesterday, pointed out on the wagering that wagering losses are admittedly deductible as against wagering gains, recognizing Well, why? Because the whole object of the Internal Revenue Code is to tax a man's net income. That's right. But still, we must, we still present it here with defining the limits as to what expenses can be deducted. And I think that those limits, you can use public policy, you can use legality or illegality, not in the sense that the lower courts have used it, or not in the sense that the government is going to urge here, as an independent ground for disallowing the deduction, not at all, but to find in the context of what is proscribed by the state, what do the people in this very industry normally, commonly, frequently find it necessary to do? Now you take... What do you mean by that? You mean that they find it normally necessary for them to violate the law? Positively. Now that's absolutely right. What do you base that on? Well, you take our very case, Your Honor. The tank truck case involves motor carriers of bulk liquid, that is, gasoline, kerosene, the fuel oils. All the equipment in the taxable year, 1951, was completely standardized by reason of the fact that during the World War II years, there were restrictions on the production of steel and on the making of these tank trucks, of the trailer trucks, so that a uniform size of tank, some 4,500 to 5,000 gallons, was the only type of equipment available and the only type of equipment used in the taxable year. The rates of the entire industry are predicated upon the carriage of a minimum of 4,500 gallons. Pennsylvania, for reasons of its own, of all the other states with which our industry operated, and we represent, in this case, the substantial carriers of the substantial amount of bulk liquids in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, West Virginia, Ohio. Pennsylvania, of all these states, had a maximum weight of 45,000 gallons. All the other states had some 60,000 gallons, gallons, pounds, pounds, pounds. The weights of the liquids were, of course, standardized. Whenever our carriers carried anything but gasoline, they were over the weight set in Pennsylvania. So whenever obviously, and we carried gasoline in the summer some 35% of the times, in the winter only 25. So between 65 and 75% of the time that we either came into Pennsylvania or left Pennsylvania for one of the other states, we were violating the Pennsylvania weight limitation law. We knew it. We had to buy it. Now why did we find it necessary? As I say, there was a question, could we have increased the rates? I think the government will concede what the tax court found, that if we, our particular company, had increased the rates, this would have referred the business to the other carriers. We would have gone out of business, the exact phrase. if the well, now, of course, the Lilly case, Boyd had answered that argument. If you recall, the Lilly case was an optician who, opticians were making kickbacks to physicians and the argument was that, well, if this optician, this taxpayer, had refused to make the kickbacks, then he would have been referred to other opticians, and the argument was, well, then all of them would have refused. Well, it so happens that in economic reality, if we had increased the rates, the others would have continued to operate the same, and we would have gone out of business. But the answer is just as well for the others. Insofar as the industry is concerned, it was impossible for the industry to increase the rates. The rates are so geared to the railroad rates and are so geared to the rates of private carriers, that is, the oil companies themselves have private, have their own fleet of trucks. We're the over-the-road industry. We don't carry just within a municipality, but within a state, from one city to another, or interstate, of course. the carriers need to weight trucks? No, sir. This is bad. The long established, complete practice in Pennsylvania was to fill the trucks to capacity to have this 4,500 gallons of freight, of oil, of liquid, pardon me, and inevitably when anything was carried other than gasoline, they were in violation of the weight laws of Pennsylvania, though completely permissible, within the weight set by the other states. I'm traveling a little. I'm making pardon me. Surely. I'm just going to ask you this. Then you take the position that you have the right to defy the state of Pennsylvania, to tell them that you will not conform to their laws, that you will drive your trucks in any way that you desire over their roads, and that when you are prosecuted and convicted of it, that you can deduct that as an expense, ordinary business expense. Well, yes. I mean, but of course I wouldn't present it in the way that your honor did. That's just what you're saying. You're saying if you can't then you won't. Well, I say this. I think it's not to be cast in that way. Well, cast it in your own way. I think that when a state prescribes certain activity and the weight laws say that we must, and the industry an unquestionably reputable, important industry, determines that it cannot economically survive under this proscription of the state, and therefore it incurs expenses which are unavoidable under its determination that it either has to remain in business or go out of business, then for revenue purposes the government, the tax laws are not to doubly punish. We've paid the fine once. Justice Burton had asked Mr. Harmwood, well, aren't you getting the government to pay part of your fine? Well, in a sense, yes, but the government in a sense pays part of every expense. I mean, the government pays part of the salary expense, of the oil expense. We can obtain permits under certain circumstances. But Congress might be certainly reluctant to pay a fine to escape. It might, very well might, and if Congress so determines, I think then possibly we would have a different question that is here Congress. Are you saying that so far as morals are concerned, you are just as high-minded as the high-minded people who violated the Volstead Act? And so long as it's on the books, you suffer the consequences of being prosecuted for that delinquency. That's exactly right. But that doesn't answer whether or not it is this kind of an expense. Yeah, that's exactly right. And you would carry that then under that theory to any kind of offense that a businessman might commit. One moment you take the position that we're a high-minded organization and everybody knows that we're moral and so forth and transacting an honorable business, and the next minute you say that you can buy the law as the liquor violators violated it. So would it make any difference to you whether you are in this legitimate trucking industry or whether you are in an underworld activity that there's no question about the legitimacy. No, Your Honor, I don't think it makes any difference. If you use the concept of ordinary and necessary, if you use that concept, and if you find in this particular industry, in this trade, in this business, it is ordinary and necessary to make these expenditures, which are in violation of the law, or to commit certain activities for which you are fined, then it makes no difference whether this is a legitimate, recognized industry, or an illegitimate one, or one which is prohibited. Yes, we take the narcotic traffic or the liquor traffic, and if the state has laws, and if one state has laws that are more stringent than its neighbors, and they use them to stop the narcotic or liquor traffic, you say that because it's necessary to keep up with your competitors, and to do business in an active way in that state, and in order to prevent you from going out of business, that you have the right to defy the laws of that state, pay your fines, and then claim them as a deduction from the government. Yes, that's right. Does it follow because what the Catholic Church calls venial offenses of committed, that therefore every venial, every petty violation of law has a moral stigma to it? No, it does not follow. I thought our whole law and all our ethics makes a difference. That doesn't mean that, I don't, that Well, of course we would take the position, but I think... Well, when you kill about 40,000 people on our highways, largely because of the use of these big trucks on highways... Well, that's not so, Your Honor. I mean... But that's a difference of opinion. Well, it is, but not on the use... You must remember in this particular case, Pennsylvania, of all the states, had a 45,000 pound limitation. Every other state had 60. Pennsylvania now has 60. There are some of them that now have 100 and some of them that have 60 in various parts of the country. And it depends upon the kind of roads that they're able to build. And if they build roads that will only support 60,000 and the trucking concerns come in and defy the laws of the state and tear them to pieces and carry weights on them that are liable to shift in a manner that on curves and so forth, in a manner that will take human life, you don't call that hardly an inconsequential thing. No, I wouldn't call it. I mean, if what you say is so, I would not at all call it an inconsequential thing. But I would say I don't see where the revenue code has any play in this. That's a different thing. That's right. I mean, and I think, Your Honor, that if the facts exist as you have indicated, you will not find the trucking industry doing commonly and normally and ordinarily the things which you've mentioned. And they don't do that. They don't do that. All trucking people do not violate the law with impunity. Absolutely. There are some who will not hire men, who will not hire men, who violate the law. And there are others who defy the law openly, as you have suggested they have the right to do. But there's no question. In Pennsylvania, when we had any interstate shipment, we were, insofar, we couldn't carry the 45,000 pounds and operate at all in Ohio and Delaware and New Jersey and be in business for a week. What do you do between the other states where one has 60,000 and the other has 100,000? Well, we didn't run into any of that problem here. Our problem here was that all the states had an approximate $60,000 weight limit except Pennsylvania. And insofar as a shipment originated in Pennsylvania or Pennsylvania was the destination, it was impossible to comply with the weight law. Well, you, I've heard it said, but I don't know. What is the authority for saying that this was a statewide within Pennsylvania? Well, I think that the tax court so found and the testimony so indicated, you see, we actually. What is the finding that it was statewide? Commonwide? Yes, yes. Not that a lot of people did, but that that was an industry infraction. Industry infraction. In fact, we represented the industry. We actually, the tank truck in the sense that we are not certificated carriers. We leased our equipment. There were three big carriers in this industry in the eastern area. So the industry is three? The industry was 85% of the business is carried by three carriers. What about the other 15? Is there any evidence in the right? No, no evidence of the other. How long was this? Did I infer from what you said a minute ago that the law has been changed in Pennsylvania? Yes, 1955. And how long was it under the 45 or 40,000? From 1943. From 1943 to 55. To 55. Going far afield, but just as a student of legislation, what efforts were made by the Investor? That's all in the record. Every two years, a new weight bill was introduced and defeated for purposes of which we think we know, but eventually it was passed. But aren't those things largely determined by the kind of highways that they build in the states and the kind of highways depend upon the amount of money they have and the number of highways they need? Positively. I mean, we're not in any way attacking the wisdom of the Pennsylvania weight led legislation. One of your truck drivers is arrested for speeding in one of these trucks. Is that the... Do you deduct that? No. Is that fine? We don't pay it. You don't reimburse him? No. You don't, but do not some truck type people? Maybe they do, yes. Maybe they do. I mean, I think it could be answered. I mean, I think you take the concept of what is ordinary and what is necessary. And if you find that it is ordinary in this particular industry to speed, then I think that so far as tax purposes are concerned, this is deductible. But your honors, I'd like the industry by determining on its own motion the extent to which it will violate the law can determine for income tax purposes what is ordinary and necessary. Well, I would say in so far as we have no limitations set forth in the statute, no regulation whatsoever which covers this matter, then we're bound by the phrase what is an ordinary and necessary business expenditure. And it's a common, usual, frequent, necessary to this industry. Your honors, I'd like to, since I just have a few minutes left, I'd like to point out one or two things. The concept of frustration has no bounds whatsoever. Because if you say that to allow the deduction of this fine would frustrate, interfere with the policy set forth by the weight limitation laws, then even more so does it interfere with those policies to allow the deduction of the driver's salaries, to allow the depreciation on the vehicles, to allow us to deduct any expenditure involved in the operation of this business. And that, of course, comes to the position that former attorney Brownell had taken when he addressed the American Bar Association to a position which the government in the petition for certiorari was reaching to take, but which they refrained from in their brief. And that is that whenever you have an illegal business, or whenever you have, say, a transgression of a legal business, you tax the entire gross income, not the net income, because to allow any expenditure, any expenditure as a deduction for tax purposes, allows this activity to continue in existence. And therefore, if you want to use the revenue law to enforce these state laws, then disallow all expenses whatsoever. And I think, Your Honors, it's very important to note that not only is there nothing in the code, but there is nothing in the regulations at all to cover this matter. But the regulations do have a penalty provision. At the time this doctrine was being evolved in the courts about frustrating public policy, one of the circuits decided the case that penalty payments paid for violation of the federal income tax laws, such as the fraud payment or the negligence or the delinquency payments, were not deductible as unnecessary in ordinary business expense, though they felt there might be some doubt about it. And thereafter, the Treasury incorporated in the regulations this penalty provision, and it is limited to penalty payments made in connection with violation of the federal income tax law. Now, of course, that's a totally different problem. We don't deny that Congress, on one hand, can make a determination and therefore, in order to aid in the enforcement of its own laws, can deny income tax recognition to a lot of things. But that's not our problem. Our problem is, are we to take an absolute determination by the state? Pennsylvania has a blue law, which is now sought to be enforced. And the commissioner of the Seventh Circuit in the Doyle case pointed this out. law, insofar as some of the Pennsylvania dealers may now sell on Sundays, in violation of the Pennsylvania law, which has been on the books for 200 years, and which has been always violated, are they not to be allowed their normal, usual, common expenses of operating on a Sunday, whereas in other states this activity is permitted, and there's no question, and it's... No. And the government, maybe not in this particular case, but in the arguments before the lower courts, in a variety of cases, sees no difference whatsoever in that situation. There is no basis for that, Your Honor, and not that some fines were allowed. Insofar as the penalty payment is made to the government for an innocent violation, they allow the deduction to be taken. The government in those cases has lost, but has argued that there is no difference whatsoever between the cost of goods sold to allow the taxpayer to deduct the illegal payment in cost of goods, or to deduct illegal penalty payments. They've argued, they've lost those cases, and I think that you will see, Your Honor, that insofar as this matter has evolved in the courts, there is no pattern whatsoever. And hence, what we must do is to limit ourselves to the concept of ordinary and necessary within the framework of the decisions of the court. Mr. Solicitor General. Mr. Chief Justice. May it please the court. The issue in this case is what ordinary and necessary means, and it is the position of the government that this court should not put its stamp of approval upon allowing the deduction under the guise or theory of ordinary and necessary, the various charges that a lawbreaker incurs in running his business. Now, the effect of such an action is obvious, if you will follow me, regarding the economics of the situation. We are not for a moment saying the federal government should take upon itself the job of enforcing all of the state laws of this country. It has enough of a problem as it is. But we are saying that this court should not approve in any way or intrude upon the sound decisions of the lower courts, where they say that you can't violate the laws of the federal government or the state and then charge off, to the extent of the federal tax, the cost of that violation and thereby frustrate or reduce the penalty conceived by the states and defeat the enforcement of their laws. Now, that's the issue. In this case of the tank truck companies, they entered upon a deliberate plan over a term of years to violate the laws of the state of Pennsylvania. And they want the United States government and in the end result the rest of the taxpayers of this country to pay that bill. What about the preceding case where you haven't got that element? The preceding case, we do not have a willful violation. The court did not make a finding, but the government's willing to concede that there was not a willful violation. We do not concede that there were not ways that they could avoid if they wanted to pay the price. Now, the problem you have in the preceding case is that there's about $28,000 of fines. And these laws are not just made to protect the roads or to get enough money so the state can replace a road that a truck breaks down because it violates these laws. They're made for two reasons. That's one of them. The other reason is to protect the life and safety of the people who travel on those roads. And the courts have so held constantly. And the court of Pennsylvania and the Third Circuit and other cases have held explicit that that's the purpose of these laws. Now, when you take a truck and you overload one of the actions, there isn't any question of what you're going to keep pounding and pounding on that part of the truck and do greater damage than if you spread that load. And that's the reason for that particular provision of the law. They say that they're so busy picking up different packages from over the countryside that they can't take and use a scale on those packages. They just take the weight of the man that wants to put any kind of waste that he may have taken in good faith, maybe without proper care and toss it in the truck and proceed. And that's one of the reasons that's been given by counsel and shown in the record for their having overweight on the one axle in violation of this law. Another is that their weight shifts during the shift over the road. And they say that can't be avoided. Now, if the fines were large enough so that it would cut into their net profit in a very substantial way and they could use, they could see that they might save it, don't you think they could put a scale out in the countryside and take a couple minutes to weigh it and see that they didn't violate this law?
